summary: Describes the protocol-agnostic congestion management system of Comcast Cable, deployed by the end of 2008. It is informational and historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A cable internet company explained how it handles busy times by treating heavy users differently, regardless of which program they use.

questions: how do cable isps manage traffic
subtitle: A broadband ISP's transparent, protocol-neutral approach to managing network congestion.

tldr.problem: Cable broadband networks are shared; when a few heavy users consume disproportionate bandwidth, it degrades service for everyone else. Comcast's old system managed congestion by targeting specific applications, which raised fairness concerns.
tldr.mechanism: This protocol-agnostic system monitors network port utilization; when a port nears congestion and a user is consuming over 70% of their provisioned bandwidth for 15 minutes, that user's traffic is downprioritized. Normal priority resumes when usage drops.
tldr.outcome: Deployed by Comcast from end of 2008 onwards. The approach influenced industry debate about fairness, transparency, and network management practices.

facts.label: Deployment scale
facts.value: Over 15 million subscribers at time of publication

today: RFC 6057 is Historic. While the protocol-agnostic approach was an important step toward transparent, fair congestion management, the broader debate about network neutrality, traffic management, and regulatory frameworks has evolved significantly since 2008. Modern ISPs use a variety of congestion management techniques, and the principles described here remain influential in industry discussions of fairness and transparency.

sections.title: The Cable Congestion Problem
sections.content:
Comcast is a large cable broadband Internet Service Provider (ISP). Its cable network is shared: many customers' cable modems connect to a single Cable Modem Termination System (CMTS) port. When network usage is light, each customer gets their provisioned speed. But at peak times, aggregate demand can exceed capacity. A small number of heavy users can degrade the experience of many others on the same port.

Previously, Comcast used a system that targeted specific peer-to-peer (P2P) applications, which drew criticism as unfair and protocol-specific. In response, Comcast designed a new protocol-agnostic system: instead of examining what application data is in a packet, it looks only at how much bandwidth each user is consuming. This RFC documents that system, deployed by December 31, 2008.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a library with one checkout line shared by 200 people. If one person checks out 50 books at once while others wait, the line backs up. Comcast's system does not care what books (data) you are checking out; it just sees if you are taking too many and politely asks you to wait if the line is getting long.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Monitoring
sections.content:
Comcast's cable network uses a hybrid fiber-coax (HFC) architecture: fiber connects the headend and CMTS (routers) to Optical Nodes in neighborhoods, and coaxial cable connects those nodes to cable modems in homes. A CMTS port typically serves 275 cable modems downstream and 100 upstream, though this varies. The system monitors traffic at the CMTS port level—the bottleneck where congestion most likely occurs.

New software deployed near regional network routers measures CMTS port utilization in real time using IPDR (Internet Protocol Detail Record) servers. When a port's aggregate traffic exceeds a Port Utilization Threshold for a specified duration, the system enters a Near Congestion State and begins examining individual users' consumption.
sections.plainLanguage: The cable company watches many checkout lines (CMTS ports). When one line starts getting crowded, a manager looks more carefully at who is checking out the most books.

sections.title: Traffic Prioritization and QoS Levels
sections.content:
All traffic from a cable modem is marked as one of two QoS levels: Priority Best Effort (PBE) or Best Effort (BE). By default, all traffic is PBE. Traffic is changed to BE only when two conditions are met: (1) the CMTS port is in a Near Congestion State, and (2) the user's consumption exceeds 70% of their provisioned upstream or downstream bandwidth averaged over a 15-minute window.

When the network is not congested, BE traffic experiences no delay or loss. Only if actual congestion occurs are BE packets delayed or dropped before PBE packets. Once a user's consumption drops below the threshold, their traffic returns to PBE. This design ensures fairness without penalizing users at off-peak times.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of checkout: normal (everyone uses it), and slow (only if the line is really long and you are checking out lots of books). Most of the time, even slow checkout is fast.

sections.title: Thresholds and User-Specific Metrics
sections.content:
The Port Utilization Threshold is 70% for upstream and 80% for downstream, measured over a 15-minute window. These thresholds trigger the Near Congestion State, not actual packet loss. The User Consumption Threshold is 70% of each user's provisioned bandwidth (not a fixed speed)—thus a customer with 22 Mbps downstream has a threshold of about 15.4 Mbps. This consumption-based approach means that activities like VoIP, HD video, or gaming alone do not typically trigger throttling; only sustained heavy-use patterns across multiple applications at once do.

Field trials in five markets showed that on any given day, less than one-third of one percent of subscribers were marked as BE. Most subscribers never experience downprioritization.
sections.plainLanguage: The system uses the internet speed you paid for as the measuring stick. If you bought 22 Mbps and use more than 15.4 Mbps for 15 minutes straight when the line is busy, you might slow down. Normal streaming or video calls do not reach that level.

sections.title: Deployment and Industry Response
sections.content:
Comcast deployed this system across all markets by the end of 2008, with servers near regional network routers managing thousands of CMTS ports and over 15 million subscribers. The system uses PacketCable Multimedia (PCMM) technology to enforce QoS policies. Cable modem firmware (bootfiles) was updated to recognize PBE and BE traffic classes, requiring no customer action.

The protocol-agnostic approach and published thresholds were designed to address FCC concerns about fairness and transparency that had arisen from the earlier application-targeted system. However, the RFC itself became an Informational (not Standards Track) document and is now Historic, as subsequent work on congestion management and network neutrality has evolved the debate beyond this specific system.
sections.plainLanguage: Comcast told the world exactly how the system works and what numbers it uses, unlike the old secret system. Other cable companies and networks can build similar systems if they wish.
